articles.headline: Thanksgiving Proclamation.
articles.text:
Territory of Dakota, Executive Office.

In accordance with a long established custom the president of the United States has set apart Thursday, the 26th day of November as a day of national Thanksgiving and gratitude to Almighty God for his manifold blessings during the year.

The citizens of the territory have more than ordinary cause for thankfulness. Though ill fortune has attended some, the masses have been abundantly blessed.

Peace and plenty are upon the land and prosperity in all its borders.

It is a season for gratitude, for benevolence, for charity. It is the day for the prodigal to be welcomed, for differences to be reconciled, for injuries to be forgiven.

I recommend therefore that the day designated by the president, be observed throughout the territory by ceasing from toil and by appropriate services in church and home. Let kindly deeds towards the suffering and destitnte, and tender sympathy for those who are in sickness and trouble distinguish our observance of this gracious time. Forgetting the strifes and enmities of life let us open wide the doors of charity and good will, remembering that "One touch of nature makes the whole world kin."

Given under my hand and the great seal of the territory, this sixth day of November, in the year of our Lord one thousand eight hundred and eighty five.

Gilbert A. Pierce.
articles.summary: Governor Gilbert A. Pierce's territorial Thanksgiving proclamation for Thursday, November 26.

articles.text: There are 24,705 men and 2,154 officers in the United States army. It certaiuly speaks well for our country that order is maintained here at less cost than any country on the globe of any considerable importance.
articles.summary: Editorial note on the small size and low cost of the U.S. army.

articles.text: Captain Lee, acting agent of the Cheyenne and Arapahoe reservations telegraphed Commissioner Atkins that all cattle have been removed from the reservations, that thousands of cattle have been turned loose in Oklahoma and that a hundred and twenty boomers have been arrested.
articles.summary: Report that all cattle have been removed from the Cheyenne and Arapahoe reservations.

articles.text: Louis Riel was executed at Regina, N. W. T. on Monday. At present, only associated press reports are at hand and as they have all along been inimical to Riel only a one-sided story is told. The greatest care has been taken to guard against the escape of the prisoner and the execution was not public. It is difficult as yet to tell what the effect will be on the half-breed population but if they do not glorify him into a martyr and at some time again strike for their rights with "Remember Riel" as a battle cry, many prophecies will be unfulfilled. Riel was perfectly calm to the last and his death was instantaneous. He left no property but bequeathes blessings and good will to men.
articles.summary: Editorial comment on the execution of Louis Riel at Regina.

articles.headline: Additional Local.
articles.text: Rassie Deffebach was in town Monday from the Bad Lands cattle Co's. ranch.
articles.summary: Rassie Deffebach in town from the Bad Lands Cattle Co. ranch.

articles.text: The dance at the Northern Pacific last Monday euening was well attended and everyone enjoyed themselves thoroughly until a late hour.
articles.summary: Well-attended dance at the Northern Pacific.

articles.text: Frank Filbert was thrown from his horse last Monday and had his collar-bone broken and his shoulder badly smashed. The accident will probably lay him up for some time.
articles.summary: Frank Filbert badly hurt when thrown from his horse.

articles.text: Willard & Keeler have as neat a meat-market as one would wish to see. Their advertisement, appearing in this issue, is an indication of the kind of stock they will keep on hand.
articles.summary: Notice of Willard & Keeler's new meat market.

articles.text: A brand-new brick-maker has appeared at the house of Peter Book. It put in an appearance Tuesday and by the way Pete is walking on clouds, it appears to be a very welcome arrival.
articles.summary: Birth of a child at the home of Peter Book.

articles.text: T. W. Gordon has received a stock of men's, ladies' and children's boots and shoes that for variety will compare favorably with any stock on the line. A call is sure to result in finding what you want.
articles.summary: T. W. Gordon receives new stock of boots and shoes.

articles.text: The last delivery of Hashknife cattle occurred last Sunday morning, completing their contract with the Ref. Car Co. Sunday's delivery was five hundred and the average was 1050.
articles.summary: Final delivery of Hashknife cattle to the Refrigerator Car Co.

articles.text: Jos. Ferris and J. C. Fisher have opened up a feed stable back of Ferris' grocery, to which they invite the attention of all. The best of care will be taken of all horses entrusted to their care, and an abundance of feed guaranteed.
articles.summary: Jos. Ferris and J. C. Fisher open a feed stable.

articles.text: Too late for last issue, we learned of the marriage of Jos. Knutson to Miss Anderson of Belfield. The wedding took place in Belfield at the home of the bride's parents. The most cordial expressions of good-will follow the newly married couple from their many friends. They are now keeping house at the Knutson creek ranch.
articles.summary: Marriage of Jos. Knutson and Miss Anderson at Belfield.

articles.text: There were three suspicious characters lurking about on the river lately, and it was thought that they were horse-thieves. No horses are known to be stolen and although there has been considerable talk on the subject, we doubt if the men took any. For a long time, no horses have been stolen in the Bad Lands and a horse-thief must be considerable of a tenderfoot to ply his vocation here.
articles.summary: Three suspected horse-thieves seen on the river; no horses known stolen.

articles.text: Colonel Malone, stock agent for the Milwaukee road, was on the train Sunday morning bound for Chicago. He says that the shipping of cattle on the N. P. is finished for this year.

articles.summary: Montana Stockgrowers' Association leaders pass through Medora.

articles.text: The management of the Southern Pacific Railroad instructed the section hands to make note of the marks and brands of cattle killed along the line of that road. Out in Uvalde County a section hand made the following report of a dead cow: "A little piece out of one ear, two little pieces out of the other ear, and a burnt place on the side."—[Texas Stockgrower.
articles.summary: Clipped anecdote about a Southern Pacific section hand's brand report.

articles.text: An Aberdeen-Angus steer, owned by J. J. Hill of St. Paul, took first prize at the Chicago Fat stock show over all competitors. There is no question that the Aberdeen-Angus are at least the equal of any cattle in beef-making qualities. When we add to this their shaggy coat impenetrable to cold, their gentle disposition, their inability to harm one another owing to lack of horns and their rustling disposition only equalled by Texas cattle, it requires no prophet to fore-tell that they are the range cattle of the future. They are making more rapid headway in public opinion than any breed has done heretofore and a very strong point in their favor is that every owner immediately becomes an enthusiast.
articles.summary: J. J. Hill's Aberdeen-Angus steer wins at Chicago; the paper predicts the breed is the range cattle of the future.

articles.text: Last Tuesday we received a visit from M. Wadsworth, Manager of the Bad Lands cattle Co., who wished the following facts published, in answer to the communication in last week's Cow Boy: When this animal in question, together with a number of others was originally branded, the work was done hurriedly and as a consequence, many were branded too deeply. The brands on twenty or more suppurated badly and the animals were kept up for better care. The particular animal in question was kept for a long time at the home ranch corrall and on account of the care it required, became well-known to several persons. The brand not only suppurated freely, but worms got in under the skin, and necessited cutting it several times. Of course this, together with the suppuration, blotched the brand. The reason the animal was not claimed this spring was that Mr. Wadsworth's representatives who saw the animal when it was caught up were new men and unacquainted with the facts. Frank Filbert, who was with the round-up, knew the animal and all the circumstances of the branding, but did not happen to be present when the animal was caught up. This was the reason she was not claimed at the spring round-up. During his own beef round-up this summer, Mr. Wadsworth, seeing the animal, had her branded again, as he considered he had a perfect right to do, knowing the animal so well. With reference to his manner of settling the case, he says it is very manifest that some one is in the wrong and he wants the result of this wrong-doing to be finally settled, as no committee on arbitration would legally have the power to do. He is perfectly willing to suffer for any wrong he has done and wants the blame settled in a final manner.
articles.summary: M. Wadsworth of the Bad Lands Cattle Co. answers last week's communication about a disputed rebranded animal.

articles.summary: Frank Moore sold the KC cattle at St. Paul.

articles.text: Charlie Bronson writes us from Chadron that he is doing well there and that the town is booming.
articles.summary: Letter from Charlie Bronson at Chadron.

articles.text: Jos. O'Brien is in Buffalo Gap, a new town on the Black Hills branch of the Northwestern. He has a black-smith shop, but the business there is over-done and he contemplates moving.
articles.summary: Jos. O'Brien blacksmithing at Buffalo Gap.

articles.text: T. G. Jones, well known here is now in Spearfish with John Guild, the backer of the Hay creek coal road. It looks as though that project may develop eventually.
articles.summary: T. G. Jones with John Guild of the Hay creek coal road at Spearfish.

articles.text: Charlie Eaton writes from Pittsburgh that he is enjoying himself hugely and will stay some time longer in the Smoky City. By the way, it changes the subject, but this name is likely to prove a mis-nomer to Pittsburgh, as the introduction of natural gas for fuel has already decreased the smoke fifty per cent.
articles.summary: Charlie Eaton writes from Pittsburgh.

articles.text: Jack Matlock writes us from Lavina, Montana, where he is driving on the stage line between Billings and Fort Benton. He says that he has a forty-mile drive through a fine agricultural and stock country. There is plenty of water and as fine timber as one would want in the Bull mountains. Money is plenty there and Jack has his share.
articles.summary: Jack Matlock driving stage in Montana.

articles.text: As we have a constitutional objection to working on a National holiday, the Cow Boy, barring accidents, will appear next Wednesday instead of Thursday. The editor-in-chief, business manager, associate editors, reporters, foreman, printers and his Satanic Majesty will all take a holiday to eat Thanksgiving turkey.
articles.summary: Next issue to appear Wednesday because of Thanksgiving.

articles.text: Nothing has been heard of J. B. Walker and all his goods that he left have been seized by the sheriff to satisfy executions issued against them for unpaid labor bills. The sale is to come off on the 25th. of this month. Numerous other unpaid bills have come to light, making the amount of his indebtedness in the neighborhood of $2,000.
articles.summary: J. B. Walker's goods seized for unpaid bills; sheriff's sale set for the 25th.

articles.text: A letter received from A. C. Huidekoper expresses his strong opinion that the future of horse-raising in this country is a bright one, especially with high-priced horses. Next summer he intends putting up a barn at the Logging camp like the one at the Deep creek horse ranch. Such expressions of confidence, coming from a keen business man and practical stockgrower like Mr. Huidekoper mean much for the future of the Bad Lands.
articles.summary: A. C. Huidekoper predicts a bright future for horse-raising and plans a barn at the Logging camp.

articles.text: Fred. Ertel, well-known on the line of the Northern Pacific is making a great success of his pictorial paper, "The St. Louis Whip." It is gotten up in "Puck" style and some of the hits are as good as any we have seen. Notably the cartoons on Cleveland ordering the cowmen off the Cheyenne and Arapahoe reservations and the appeal of the Territories for admission into the Union, which now adorn the walls of the Cow Boy office.
articles.summary: Fred. Ertel's pictorial paper The St. Louis Whip; its cartoons hang in the Cow Boy office.

articles.text: We have refrained from remarks on Rev. Mr. Schaffner of Dickinson, hoping that we could find some good to say. During his many visits here, he did not impress our people favorably. He was too much "on the make." A ministers ruling passion should by no means be a love of gain but Mr. Schaffner's certainly was. Lately he had another fight with a neighbor on account of which his bondsmen went back on him. Deputp Sheriff Drury arrested him, but gave him considerable freedom in searching for new bondsmen, on his solemn promise not to escape. His solemn promise seemed to have little effect for it looks now as if he had skipped the country. We suggest that the officers look for him in his old home in Canuckland.
articles.summary: Rev. Mr. Schaffner of Dickinson appears to have skipped the country after arrest.

articles.text: S. G. Miller of New York and a representative of New York capitalists arrived Tuesday night and is awaiting the return of the Marquis from his hunting trip down the river. He is here to look up the feasibility of building a rail-road to the Belle Fourche, where the plan must be to connect with the prospective Hay creek coal road. The New York capitalists are in earnest about the road and a favorable report from Mr. Miller will probably set the project in motion. The Northern Pacific is actively interested in the plan and will give it every encouragement. For many reasons, we would not be at all surprised if we would inside of two years, have direct railroad connections with the Black Hills.
articles.summary: S. G. Miller of New York arrives to study a railroad to the Belle Fourche and awaits the Marquis de Morès.

articles.text: Two of the petitions for county organization are now in, containing more than enough names, according to law, for the organization of the county. The petition for down the river is not yet in, but is known to contain a goodly number of names. No names have as yet been secured from the Beaver creek country as it is not certain where the territorial line runs. The sentiment there is, however, entirely in favor of organization. The manner of organizing counties was changed last winter as follows: The number of signatures on the petition must be 150 instead of fifty. The Governor is then authorized to appoint two officers of the senior county, in our case this is Morton Co., who shall divide the county into voting precincts and appoint three judges of election who shall divide the county into commissioners districts and appoint a day for the general election of county officers. All this will take some time and the work cannot be delayed.
articles.summary: Petitions for organizing the county are coming in.
